articles.headline: OFAC Issues Counter Narcotics and Cyber-related Designations, Amends Russia-related General License
body: The Office of Foreign Assets Control (OFAC) announced new designations targeting individuals and entities involved in counter narcotics and cyber-related illicit activities. This action underscores the U.S. government's ongoing commitment to disrupting global criminal networks that pose a threat to national security.

In conjunction with these designations, OFAC issued an Illicit Drugs General License to ensure that legitimate transactions are not unduly impacted. Additionally, an existing Russia-related General License was amended, and new Frequently Asked Questions (FAQs) were published to provide further guidance to the public regarding the scope and application of these measures.

These measures aim to enhance the effectiveness of U.S. sanctions programs by targeting key facilitators of illicit trade and cybercrime, while also providing clarity and flexibility for legitimate humanitarian and commercial activities.

articles.headline: OFAC Imposes New Counter Terrorism Designations
body: The Office of Foreign Assets Control (OFAC) today announced new designations under its counter terrorism authority. These actions target individuals and entities determined to have provided material support to, or acted on behalf of, designated terrorist organizations.

These designations are part of a broader effort to disrupt the financial networks of terrorist groups and limit their ability to plan and carry out attacks. The U.S. government remains committed to using all available tools to combat terrorism globally.

Further details regarding the specific individuals and entities designated were made available on the Treasury Department's website, emphasizing the ongoing vigilance against threats to international security.

articles.headline: OFAC Announces Joint Counter Narcotics and Counter Terrorism Designations
body: The Office of Foreign Assets Control (OFAC) today implemented new designations combining counter narcotics and counter terrorism authorities. This joint action targets illicit networks involved in both drug trafficking and supporting terrorist activities, highlighting the nexus between these criminal enterprises.

These designations aim to sever the financial lifelines of organizations that exploit the global financial system for their nefarious purposes. The U.S. government continues to collaborate with international partners to identify and disrupt such multifaceted threats.
The action reinforces the U.S. commitment to combating transnational criminal organizations that undermine stability and security worldwide.

articles.headline: OFAC Updates Iran Designation List
body: The Office of Foreign Assets Control (OFAC) has announced an update to its Iran designation list. This action reflects the U.S. government's ongoing efforts to address Iran's destabilizing activities and its support for terrorism.

The updated designations aim to further restrict Iran's access to the international financial system and pressure the regime to alter its behavior. Entities and individuals found to be in violation of these sanctions face severe penalties.
The Treasury Department continues to monitor developments related to Iran and will take further action as necessary to protect U.S. national security interests.

articles.headline: OFAC Imposes New Iran-related Designations
body: The Office of Foreign Assets Control (OFAC) today announced new Iran-related designations. These actions target individuals and entities involved in various aspects of Iran's illicit activities, including its proliferation of weapons of mass destruction and support for regional proxies.

These designations are part of a comprehensive strategy to exert maximum pressure on the Iranian regime. The U.S. government remains steadfast in its commitment to preventing Iran from acquiring nuclear weapons and curbing its malign influence.
Further information regarding the specific targets and the implications of these designations can be found on the Treasury Department's website.

articles.headline: OFAC Designates Cyber-related and Transnational Criminal Organizations, Issues Cuba Designations and Determination
body: The Office of Foreign Assets Control (OFAC) today announced new designations targeting cyber-related threats and transnational criminal organizations. These actions aim to disrupt malicious cyber actors and criminal networks that exploit the global financial system.

In a separate but concurrent action, OFAC also issued new designations related to Cuba, alongside the publication of a Cuba-related determination. These measures reflect the U.S. government's ongoing policy towards Cuba and its efforts to promote democracy and human rights.
The designations underscore the U.S. commitment to combating a wide range of illicit activities, from cybercrime to the suppression of democratic freedoms.

articles.headline: OFAC Imposes Iran-related Designations, Amends Venezuela-related General License
body: The Office of Foreign Assets Control (OFAC) today announced new Iran-related designations and updates to certain Iran-related listings. These actions are part of the U.S. government's continued pressure campaign against the Iranian regime.

Alongside these measures, OFAC published an Iran-related alert to inform the public about potential risks and illicit finance schemes. Additionally, an amended Venezuela-related General License and a new Frequently Asked Question (FAQ) were issued, providing updated guidance on transactions involving Venezuela.
These actions demonstrate a multifaceted approach to addressing threats from both Iran and Venezuela, aiming to prevent the circumvention of sanctions and promote compliance.

articles.headline: OFAC Issues Amended Iran-related General License
body: The Office of Foreign Assets Control (OFAC) today issued an amended Iran-related General License. This amendment aims to clarify and potentially expand the scope of permissible activities under existing sanctions, while maintaining core restrictions.

General Licenses are often issued to authorize specific types of transactions that would otherwise be prohibited, typically for humanitarian purposes or to facilitate certain legitimate commercial activities. The details of this amendment are crucial for entities engaging with Iran.
The updated guidance reflects the U.S. government's ongoing review of its sanctions programs to ensure they are effectively targeted and do not inadvertently impede legitimate trade or aid.

articles.headline: OFAC Imposes North Korea and Democratic Republic of the Congo-related Designations
body: The Office of Foreign Assets Control (OFAC) today announced new designations targeting North Korea and the Democratic Republic of the Congo (DRC). These actions aim to counter illicit activities that undermine regional stability and human rights.

The North Korea designations are part of ongoing efforts to address the regime's weapons of mass destruction programs and its illicit revenue generation. The DRC-related designations target individuals and entities involved in corruption and human rights abuses.
These measures underscore the U.S. commitment to promoting accountability and disrupting networks that threaten international peace and security.

articles.headline: OFAC Reaches Settlement Agreement with Extreme Networks, Inc.
body: The U.S. Department of the Treasury's Office of Foreign Assets Control (OFAC) announced a settlement agreement with Extreme Networks, Inc. This settlement resolves apparent violations of OFAC sanctions programs.

Settlement agreements typically involve a monetary penalty and a commitment from the company to implement enhanced compliance measures. These actions serve as a reminder to all companies of the importance of robust sanctions compliance programs.
The details of the settlement, including the specific violations and the agreed-upon penalty, are available on the OFAC website.

articles.headline: Extreme Networks, Inc. Pays $1,529,685 to Settle OFAC Sanctions Violations
body: Extreme Networks, Inc. has agreed to pay $1,529,685 to the Office of Foreign Assets Control (OFAC) to settle apparent violations of various sanctions programs. This settlement highlights the importance of robust compliance measures for companies operating internationally.

The specific details of the violations were outlined in the settlement agreement, which is publicly available. OFAC civil penalties are a key tool in enforcing U.S. sanctions laws and deterring illicit financial activities.
Companies are encouraged to review their compliance programs regularly to ensure adherence to all applicable sanctions regulations and avoid similar penalties.

articles.headline: Bank of America, N.A. Settles OFAC Sanctions Violations for $11,662,930
body: Bank of America, N.A. has reached a settlement with the Office of Foreign Assets Control (OFAC) to pay $11,662,930 for apparent violations of numerous sanctions programs, including those related to Iran, Russia, narcotics, and global terrorism.
This settlement was part of a coordinated enforcement action that also involved significant penalties from FinCEN and the OCC for Bank Secrecy Act/Anti-Money Laundering (BSA/AML) deficiencies.

The case underscores the critical need for financial institutions to maintain comprehensive and effective sanctions compliance programs to prevent illicit transactions and avoid substantial penalties.

articles.headline: Pegasus Worldwide Logistics Fined $175,015 by OFAC
body: Pegasus Worldwide Logistics has been assessed a civil penalty of $175,015 by the Office of Foreign Assets Control (OFAC). This penalty is for apparent violations of U.S. sanctions regulations.

The enforcement action serves as a reminder to logistics and shipping companies of their responsibilities in ensuring compliance with sanctions programs, particularly concerning the movement of goods and services globally.
Details of the specific violations and the terms of the settlement are available in the public enforcement information released by OFAC.

articles.headline: Individual Pays $1,427,230 in OFAC Civil Penalty
body: An individual has paid a civil penalty of $1,427,230 to the Office of Foreign Assets Control (OFAC) for apparent violations of sanctions regulations. This action highlights that OFAC enforcement extends to individuals as well as corporate entities.
The specific nature of the individual's violations was detailed in the enforcement release. Such penalties underscore the personal responsibility of individuals to adhere to U.S. sanctions laws.
OFAC continues to pursue enforcement actions against those who violate sanctions, regardless of whether they are part of a larger organization or acting independently.

articles.headline: IMF Head Warns AI Demand Will Drive Global Interest Rate Hikes
body: Kristalina Georgieva, Managing Director of the International Monetary Fund (IMF), has cautioned that surging demand for artificial intelligence (AI) will compel central banks worldwide to increase interest rates. Speaking at the 2026 APEC summit in Shenzhen, Georgieva stated that the demand for AI hardware and related technology products is contributing to rising consumer prices globally.

This inflationary pressure, coupled with the energy shock from the ongoing conflict in the Middle East, necessitates a tightening of monetary policy in many economies. Georgieva projected global inflation to reach 4.7% this year, noting that the rapid deployment of AI is also fueling stronger-than-expected economic growth in several countries despite geopolitical headwinds.

Central banks, including the European Central Bank, the US Federal Reserve, and the Bank of England, have already raised rates this year due to oil prices exceeding $100 a barrel. Financial markets anticipate further rate increases next year as AI bolsters economic growth amidst a volatile global landscape.

articles.headline: OCC Adjusts Civil Money Penalties for Inflation in 2026
body: The Office of the Comptroller of the Currency (OCC) submitted a notice to the Federal Register to adjust the maximum amount of each civil money penalty (CMP) within its jurisdiction. This adjustment is mandated by the Federal Civil Penalties Inflation Adjustment Act of 1990, as amended by the 2015 Adjustment Act.

The adjusted maximum penalties are effective as of January 10, 2025, for violations occurring on or after November 2, 2015. The OCC will continue to use the CMP limits published in January 2025 for national banks and federal savings associations for the maximum amounts that may be assessed in 2026.

This revision does not affect the OCC's discretion to assess a CMP in an amount lower than the maximum allowed. The OCC may impose inflation-adjusted maximum CMPs on any national bank or federal savings association when appropriate.

articles.headline: OCC Releases Report on Large Bank 'Debanking Activities' and Fair Banking
body: On October 14, 2026, the Office of the Comptroller of the Currency (OCC) released a report titled 'Guaranteeing Fair Banking for All Americans.' The report details a review undertaken in September 2025 of the nine largest U.S. national banks to determine if their policies or practices denied or limited access to financial services based on political or religious beliefs, affiliations, or lawful business activities.

The OCC concluded that broad reputation risk policies lacking clear standards and objective, risk-based criteria had the effect of limiting financial services access for certain persons and entities. The report noted that the OCC has removed references to reputation risk from its policy issuances and will no longer examine banks for reputation risk.

The OCC is considering further rulemaking to prevent discrimination against customers based on political or religious beliefs and is also considering guidance to clarify the risk-based application of the Bank Secrecy Act to certain customers or business activities.

articles.headline: BIS Imposes New Export Controls on Remote Access to Advanced AI Semiconductors
body: The U.S. Department of Commerce's Bureau of Industry and Security (BIS) has published an interim final rule (IFR) that immediately restricts remote access to advanced AI semiconductors. This new rule targets companies from China and other countries subject to a U.S. arms embargo, limiting their access to advanced AI semiconductors located in data centers outside the United States.

The rule also imposes new export controls on transfers of advanced AI semiconductors to or within Malaysia, Singapore, Thailand, Indonesia, and Brazil, citing a high risk of diversion to China. An exception applies to U.S.-headquartered companies, provided they submit monthly reports to BIS.

This IFR, effective upon publication in the Federal Register, aims to prevent foreign adversaries from bypassing existing controls on physical shipments of advanced chips by renting computing power through third-country data centers. It also formally rescinds the Biden administration's AI Diffusion Rule.
articles.source: Sidley Austin LLP / K&L Gates / WilmerHale

articles.headline: BIS Extends Suspension of End-User Controls for Affiliates of Certain Listed Entities
body: The Bureau of Industry and Security (BIS) has announced an extension of the suspension of the interim final rule (IFR) titled 'Expansion of End-User Controls to Cover Affiliates of Certain Listed Entities.' The suspension, which was set to expire on November 9, 2026, has now been extended through January 10, 2027.

This IFR, originally published on September 30, 2025, and subsequently stayed on November 10, 2025, aimed to expand end-user controls to include affiliates of certain listed entities. The extension provides additional time for stakeholders to adjust to potential future changes.
The decision to extend the suspension reflects BIS's ongoing evaluation of the rule's implications and its commitment to providing clarity and stability for businesses engaged in international trade.

articles.headline: Addressing Remote Access to Advanced Semiconductors
body: In this interim final rule (IFR), the Department of Commerce is establishing new rules to prevent certain foreign actors from leveraging advanced computing power based on U.S. technology to threaten U.S. national security and foreign policy interests. First, this rule establishes new restrictions which will apply for exports, reexports, or transfers (in-country) to overseas data centers that remotely supply significant volumes of compute to companies headquartered in Country Group D:5 or Macau. These restrictions will undermine the ability of companies headquartered in countries of concern from using U.S. advanced Super Intelligence (SI) semiconductors to train advanced SI models. Data centers, foreign foundries, and chip exporters are required to perform robust due diligence on their customers, including any direct or indirect ownership or control by persons in Country Group D:5 or Macau, as part of complying with this new control. The license requirement will not apply to commercial recommender systems, such as those used by online retailers or social media companies, as these functions do not pose the same national security threat. Second, in addition to the current license requirements for advanced semiconductors, a license will be required to export, reexport, or transfer (in-country) advanced semiconductors to Indonesia, Malaysia, Singapore, Thailand, or Brazil (and any additional country designated by the Secretary of Commerce, in consultation with the Secretary of State or the Assistant to the President for National Security Affairs)--countries which present a higher-than-normal risk of diversion. The license requirement for these five countries will not apply to semiconductors destined to companies headquartered in, or whose ultimate parent company is headquartered in, the United States, provided certain reporting requirements are met. Commerce will be actively monitoring for countries that tolerate evasion of this IFR and will consider a range of consequences for such countries, such as import restrictions, new license requirements on advanced semiconductor exports, downgrading the country's status in the U.S. export control regime, and Entity List designations and temporary export prohibitions for foreign persons involved in such activities. Third, this IFR amends the presumptions which front-end chips fabricators and chip packagers face when exporting advanced-node logic chips. These amendments reduce the number of pathways to overcome the presumptions for chip designers located in destinations which face a license requirement for SI chips. This change gives the U.S. government critical oversight over companies headquartered in certain countries that seek to leverage advanced semiconductor production capabilities in third countries. Finally, the IFR formally rescinds the regulations implementing the Biden-era AI Diffusion Rule. The AI Diffusion Rule has never been enforced. The regulatory changes in this rule formalize the rescission of the AI Diffusion Rule, which the Department of Commerce Bureau of Industry and Security (BIS) announced in May 2025.

articles.headline: Streamlining Export Controls for Drone Exports
body: The Bureau of Industry and Security (BIS) is easing export controls on certain Unmanned Aerial Vehicles (UAVs or drones) and related parts, components, accessories, attachments, technology, and software under the Export Administration Regulations (EAR). Specifically, this rule: eliminates wind gust tolerance as a parameter for determining UAV controls under the EAR; increases the threshold for national security controls on certain UAVs from an endurance of 30 minutes to an endurance of 3 hours; makes conforming changes to remove national security controls on software and technology associated with UAVs with an endurance less than 3 hours; maintains military end-use and end-user controls on those lower endurance drones and associated software and technology; clarifies Commerce Control List (CCL) controls for certain UAVs specially designed for military use; and removes national security controls on certain specially designed parts, components, accessories, and attachments for such UAVs as they do not provide any significant military or intelligence capabilities.
